rv.q: This latest musical adapted from one of Disney’s popular movies defied my dour expectations...“Aladdin” has an infectious and only mildly syrupy spirit. Not to mention enough baubles, bangles and beading to keep a whole season of “RuPaul’s Drag Race” contestants in runway attire.

It's spritely directed and choreographed by Casey Nicholaw, well sung by a huge 35-person cast wearing an alarming number of harem pants, and hits that sweet spot Disney Theatrical Productions do so well, a saccharine fairy tale for the kids cut by some sly, vinegary quips for their parents......
That hokey humour gives the show a welcome humanity along with the presence of Trevor Dion Nicholas, the one import from the 2014. Broadway production, as the genie.
In that regard, Aladdin delivers in abundance.
Cheerful, enjoyable, human-scale musical-comedy.

Directed and choreographed by musical comedy specialist Casey Nicholaw with loads of retro showmanship, an unapologetic embrace of casbah kitsch and a heavy accent on shtick, this is sweet, silly fun.

After a string of recent less-than-smashing Broadway adaptations, Disney wanted something it could market not only to the parents-with-children crowd but also to date-night couples looking for a few laughs.
Billing notwithstanding, the real star of 'Aladdin' is James
Disney’s new “Aladdin” doesn’t quite catch lightning in a bottle — but it lets a pretty nifty genie out of a lamp.

He is in fact–and no surprise here–the most enjoyable ingredient of director Casey Nicholaw’s production, which despite a lot of huffing and puffing and brandishing of scimitars exposes more of the material’s rough patches than it does any happier conceits.
Aside from the tonic of Iglehart’s djinn, however, Aladdin is short on magic.
If the whole enterprise is arranged to prevent us from taking anything seriously, why should we respond when we’re suddenly asked to care?
Other changes to the original material are less successful, especially the contemporary updates to book and lyrics that replace the tone of fairy-tale innocence with show-queen vulgarity.

Like so many movie-to-musicals, "Aladdin" has to move between several worlds and, while there are some lovely visual ideas here and some exuberant turns in sidekick roles, only the Genie really has figured out how to shape-shift for maximum theatrical enjoyment.
Even the most jaded observers will, again, share in his enthusiasm.
In a Broadway musical season that has so far been a bit disappointing, it's a bonus to finally see a show that has as much magic as Aladdin.
This entertaining but emotionally sparse adaptation of Disney's 1992 cartoon that won Oscars for its score and the song 'A Whole New World.'
More than four years after opening night, the musical is still a balm and a tonic—with perhaps a bit more punch nowadays.

"The musical comedy is all about one character: the Genie. But that is not the only thing worth talking about. From “Arabian Nights” to “Prince Ali,” Nicholaw uses his multicultural ensemble flawlessly, unraveling layers to each number that surprise and wonder.
Score Aladdin a considerable win for Disney, likely to fill the New Amsterdam with happy crowds for seasons to come.
It is too much to say he is the show in “Aladdin,” but he certainly gives – and deserves – some big love.
Aladdin is frisky and fun, another demonstration of Disney professionalism.
He ensures you can't look away, even though the rest of Aladdin seems determined to give you little, if anything, worth looking at or thinking about.
Too bad it doesn’t get far off the ground.
It’s a two-and-a-half hour show.

Except for an exuberant performance by James Monroe Iglehart, who plays the genie, and a production number that brings the evening some old-time Broadway pizzazz, the show is a flavorless rehash of what's been done much better before.
The stage is alive from beginning to end.
I'm happy to report that it makes the transition to stage seamlessly in a lavish and magical production that the whole family will enjoy.
The magic carpet flies smoothly and so does the rest of “Aladdin,” a buoyant musical comedy fashioned from the 1992. Disney animated feature.
Mainly, this Aladdin is F-U-N because it was so craftily assembled.
Enchanting but not extreme, magical without unnecessary fireworks, jaw-dropping without having to fly over the audience.

Aladdin, while charming and fun, lacks the enchantment and savviness of Disney’s most notable theatrical productions.
A fun treat for the kids for sure, and even the adults who loathe Disney’s theatrical presence will find themselves enjoying the show.
Here’s the thing: this production is a huge and colorful spectacle, but ultimately, I thought it lacked heart – the heart that I feel is deeply a part of the movie.

Instead, it's pleasant but forgettable.

cn.t: Critics find Aladdin a visually spectacular but formulaic Disney adaptation that delivers solid family entertainment without breaking new ground. James Monroe Iglehart's exuberant Genie performance earns widespread praise as the show's standout element.

lo.t: Lottery opens 9 AM day prior to desired performance, closes 3 PM day prior to the performance.
lo.inst: Entrants must be 18+. Tickets non-transferable. Must purchase via credit card within 60-minute window. Retrieve tickets at box office 60 minutes before performance. Limit 2.

sg.ra: Multiple guides converge on center-orchestra rows D-L as the New Amsterdam's prime zone — far enough back that the Aladdin flying-carpet rig and Cave of Wonders set pieces read cleanly, but ahead of the mezzanine overhang that begins at row P. Headout specifically flags 'Center Orchestra - Any seats in Row D to K' as premium; Tickadoo calls rows D-L the spot 'where the Cave of Wonders feels truly cavernous.' Unlike most Broadway houses, the New Amsterdam 'was, by far, the most comfortable Broadway theater visited' with 'more legroom than found in other theaters,' so center orchestra here doesn't carry the usual cramped-knee penalty.

Tripadvisor's Aladdin FAQ is explicit: 'Rows A-C are too close to the stage' and 'you may miss out on a few acts that happen at the sides.' Tickadoo warns 'First few rows may require looking up' — a real cost on a show whose magic-carpet rig flies well above eyeline. The one upside is legroom: Row A gets 'extra legroom' per SeatPlan, but that is the only reason to pick front row here and the sightline penalty outweighs it for a Disney spectacle show.

The smart discount play at the New Amsterdam. Tickadoo pitches 'Rows M through Q center' as the value zone where you see 'full scope of the production's elaborate dance numbers' — key for Friend Like Me and the Genie ensemble. Headout names 'Center Orchestra - Any seats in Row F to O' as a value option. The catch that's unique to this house: 'Mezzanine Row A overhangs at Orchestra Row P,' so rows P and especially Q start losing the top of the flying rig. Aim M-O for the best value/sightline tradeoff.

Front-center mezzanine is the specific seat that Aladdin regulars recommend over center orchestra — unusual advice for a Broadway musical, but show-specific: 'The first few rows of the center Mezzanine offer perhaps the most enchanting view of Aladdin and Jasmine's magic carpet ride, where the illusion is flawless.' From the elevated vantage the wires read as invisible and the carpet 'truly appears to soar through a star-filled night sky.' RateYourSeats calls rows AA-EE 'among the best in theatre with very clear sightlines.' One caveat: 'The safety railing and lighting rig in front of row AA may cut off parts of the stage for shorter patrons' — adult seated height clears it fine but shorter kids benefit from a booster.

A quirky feature specific to this house: SeatPlan notes 'Left and Right Mezzanine rows MM-QQ are short; far aisle seats are more central than other rows.' A Tripadvisor reviewer who sat in row PP with an 8-year-old flagged the real payoff: 'THE BEST ROW IN MEZZ IS ROW MM on the side. It is a row of 4' with a private entrance, no stairs, and a group of 4 gets the whole row — no one climbing past you. Tradeoff is obvious distance and side angle, but for a family of 4 with a small child the uninterrupted private-row setup is a genuinely unusual value play.

The best of the balcony at the New Amsterdam — a distinct third tier, not a rear mezzanine. SeatPlan: 'Rows A and B of the Center Balcony still have a fair overall view' and RateYourSeats places the best balcony sightlines in 'rows A-E closest to the center of the level.' A Tripadvisor destination expert who saw Aladdin from balcony row A called the view 'excellent' and said 'the large-scale choreography was better appreciated from the balcony's elevated position' — genuinely supports the magic-carpet-from-above case. However, 'the first row of the balcony is about as far as the last row of the Orchestra Level, but from a much higher vantage point,' and row A has a safety railing that can clip the stage bottom for shorter patrons. 'Balcony seating is the least comfortable of the theater, with limited legroom.'

RateYourSeats is direct: 'Beware of rows J or higher in the side sections. In the back of the balcony are support poles that go up to the ceiling. While these are skinny and minimally invasive, they can provide a distraction and lead to partially obstructed views.' SeatPlan names specific obstructed seats from structural poles: G11, G112, H11, J10, L12. Combine thin poles, vertigo-inducing steepness ('steep angle that may be uncomfortable for patrons suffering from vertigo'), and zero legroom — ('if you purchase a balcony ticket, you will have ZERO leg room. it makes airplane seating look spacious') — and the price savings vanish.

vr.q: This show is even more magical than I remember. I lost count of how many times I got chills from the music to the set and the magic bit moment.
